analysis.one_liner: Extends middle-class income tax rates and credits through 2013 while letting taxes rise on high incomes and large estates.
analysis.headline: The Senate's middle-class tax cut bill was introduced and placed on the calendar in July 2012 but never received a vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have extended, for one more year, the lower income tax rates and expanded tax credits (child tax credit, college tuition credit, earned income credit) that primarily benefit households making under $200,000–$250,000. To offset part of that cost, it would have let the top income tax rates rise back up on income above that level, raised the capital gains and dividend rates to 20 percent for the highest earners, and restored the estate tax to a $3.5 million exemption with a 45 percent top rate. It also patched the alternative minimum tax and extended a business equipment-expensing break. The bill was introduced by Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid in July 2012, placed on the Senate calendar, and never brought up for a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households earning under $200,000 ($250,000 for couples) would keep the lower tax rates, expanded child and college credits, and larger earned income credit for another year. Low-income families with three or more children, students claiming the tuition credit, and middle-income households at risk of the alternative minimum tax all benefit. It also helps small businesses through the equipment-expensing extension.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the 2001 and 2003 tax rate reductions and the lower dividend and capital gains rates through 2013 for taxpayers with income of $200,000 or less ($250,000 for married couples), so the typical working family's income tax rates do not jump on January 1, 2013 [S2][S3].

Extends the expanded American Opportunity college tuition tax credit, the larger refundable child tax credit, and the bigger earned income tax credit for families with three or more children — all credits that primarily help low- and middle-income households [S2][S3].
Raises income taxes on high earners by letting the top two rates apply above roughly $200,000–$250,000 and phasing out personal exemptions and itemized deductions for high incomes [S2][S3].
Restores a tougher estate tax: a $3.5 million exclusion with a 45 percent top rate, instead of the lower-tax regime then in place, meaning very large estates pay more [S2][S3].

Patches the alternative minimum tax for 2012 so millions of middle-income households are not swept into it, and continues a rule that keeps tax refunds from being counted as income when determining eligibility for federal assistance programs [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-income taxpayers would pay more: the 36 and 39.6 percent rates would apply to income above roughly $200,000–$250,000, personal exemptions and itemized deductions would phase out at those incomes, capital gains and dividends would be taxed at 20 percent for top earners, and estates above $3.5 million would face up to a 45 percent rate. Future taxpayers also bear the cost of the unpaid-for extensions.

drawbacks.text: The bill is unpaid-for: it explicitly exempts its own cost from statutory pay-as-you-go rules, meaning the lost revenue would add to the federal deficit [S2][S3].
The extension runs only through 2013, setting up the same fight again roughly a year later and leaving families and businesses uncertain what their tax bills will look like beyond that [S2].

It also extends generous business tax breaks — including the election to expense up to $250,000 in business assets — without offsetting the cost, which critics would call additional deficit spending [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivered large, concrete benefits to the overwhelming majority of taxpayers — keeping lower rates and expanded credits that were scheduled to expire — and paid for part of it by raising rates at the very top and restoring a stronger estate tax. The honest objection is that it was not fully paid for: it waived pay-as-you-go rules, so the middle-class extension added to the deficit, and a one-year extension guaranteed the same fight would recur immediately.

outcome.mechanism: Harry Reid introduced it in July 2012 and it was placed on the Senate calendar, but it was never brought up for a vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Harry Reid introduced S. 3393 on July 17, 2012 [S1][S5].
It was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on July 18, 2012 — meaning it was formally waiting for floor time [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a floor vote, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1][S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors, so no other senator put their name on it [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households and very large estates came out ahead: the bill that would have raised their income tax rates, investment-income taxes, and estate taxes never advanced, and the tax debate was resolved without this bill's terms.

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in July 2012 and placed it on the Senate calendar as the Democrats' vehicle for extending the middle-class tax cuts before the scheduled expiration.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed allowing any Bush-era tax rates to expire, including the rates above $250,000 that this bill would have let rise; the bill drew no Republican support and was never brought to the floor.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Led the Republican opposition to any tax increase on high earners during the 2012 extension fight, pushing for a full extension of all the Bush-era rates.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party; in the broader 2012 fight over the expiring tax cuts, Democrats pushed to let rates rise above roughly $250,000 while Republicans opposed letting any rates rise.

industries.note: The bill would raise their income tax rates, phase out their deductions, tax more of their investment income at 20 percent, and tax estates above $3.5 million at up to 45 percent — the direct cost of the bill.

They gain a one-year extension of the election to immediately expense up to $250,000 in equipment purchases, but like all taxpayers their rates were left in limbo past 2013 and the break is deficit-financed.
The bill's PAYGO waiver means its full cost would be added to the national debt, a cost that falls on future taxpayers.
